It is used as a proxy for phytoplankton biomass in surface waters and is a core variable for monitoring phytoplankton blooms, eutrophication status and marine ecosystem productivity. The products in this collection are derived from Sentinel-3 OLCI images at 300 m spatial resolution; each input image results in one output product.

Retrieving CHL reliably in optically complex coastal waters, such as the Belgian coastal zone, is challenging: many algorithms exist, each performing well only in some optical conditions. Lavigne et al. (2021) defined a multi-algorithm approach that automatically switches between blue-green and NIR-red band-ratio algorithms based on the water type. This approach is the basis of the Copernicus Marine multi-sensor chlorophyll-a product for the Atlantic (OCEANCOLOUR_ATL_BGC_L3_MY_009_113, 1 km), which OSPAR uses for the Quality Status Report on eutrophication in the North Sea (https://oap.ospar.org/en/ospar-assessments/quality-status-reports/qsr-2023/indicator-assessments/chl-a-concentrations/).

The products in this collection transfer this approach to Sentinel-3 OLCI at 300 m with OCTIS (Ocean Colour Transfer across Imaging Sensors), a machine-learning method trained to reproduce the Copernicus Marine CHL from the sensor's own reflectance. The remote-sensing reflectance (RRS, atmospherically corrected with ACOLITE) is assigned membership values for five optical water types. For each water type, a LightGBM model (gradient-boosted decision trees) estimates CHL from the OLCI RRS bands and band ratios, and the five estimates are blended according to the water-type memberships. The models were trained for the Aquascope region of interest, with the Copernicus Marine CHL as the training label after a recalibration to in-situ HPLC measurements from Rijkswaterstaat (NL).

Lavigne, H., Van der Zande, D., Ruddick, K., Cardoso dos Santos, J. F., Gohin, F., Brotas, V., & Kratzer, S. (2021). Quality-control tests for OC4, OC5 and NIR-red satellite chlorophyll-a algorithms applied to coastal waters. Remote Sensing of Environment, 255, 112237.

title: Aquascope turbidity (TUR), level-3, 10 m, daily
description:
Turbidity (TUR) is an optical measure of water clarity that quantifies how strongly suspended particles (sediments, phytoplankton, organic matter, etc.) scatter light, with higher turbidity indicating cloudier or more opaque water. In water-quality monitoring it is typically expressed in Formazin Nephelometric Units (FNU). The products in this collection are derived from Sentinel-2 MSI images at 10 m spatial resolution; each input image results in one output product.

Nechad et al. (2009, 2010) provided the theoretical basis for SPM and TUR as a function of reflectance at a single band. They also derived calibration coefficients for wavelengths between 520 nm and 885 nm, allowing the algorithm to be applied to any sensor with a single red or NIR band. RRS increases with TUR, but the slope and saturation point depend on the wavelength. This led to the development of 'switching single-band algorithms' using different wavelengths for different SPM concentrations. The Novoa et al. (2017) approach is applied to both SPM and TUR products across all regions, providing a multi-band product using two bands (red: 665 nm and near-infrared: 865 nm).

Nechad, B., Ruddick, K. G., & Neukermans, G. (2009). Calibration and validation of a generic multisensor algorithm for mapping of turbidity in coastal waters. Proc. SPIE 7473, Remote Sensing of the Ocean, Sea Ice, and Large Water Regions 2009, 74730H.

Nechad, B., Ruddick, K. G., & Park, Y. (2010). Calibration and validation of a generic multisensor algorithm for mapping of total suspended matter in turbid waters. Remote Sensing of Environment, 114(4), 854-866.

Novoa, S., Doxaran, D., Ody, A., Vanhellemont, Q., Lafon, V., Lubac, B., & Gernez, P. (2017). Atmospheric corrections and multi-conditional algorithm for multi-sensor remote sensing of suspended particulate matter in low-to-high turbidity levels coastal waters. Remote Sensing, 9(1), 61.

title: Aquascope suspended particulate matter (SPM), level-3, 10 m, daily
description:
Suspended particulate matter (SPM) is the mass concentration of all particles suspended in the near-surface water: mineral sediment, organic detritus and phytoplankton (g mâ3). It is a key water-quality indicator: it controls water clarity and the penetration of light, and it traces sediment transport, river plumes, dredging and resuspension. The products in this collection are derived from Sentinel-2 MSI images at 10 m spatial resolution; each input image results in one output product.

SPM is retrieved from the remote-sensing reflectance (RRS) of a single band with the algorithm of Nechad et al. (2010), which relates RRS to SPM through a semi-analytical function calibrated for wavelengths between 520 nm and 885 nm. RRS increases with SPM until it saturates, at a concentration that depends on the wavelength: the red band is sensitive at low to moderate concentrations but saturates in very turbid water, where the near-infrared band still responds. Following the switching approach of Novoa et al. (2017), the SPM of each pixel is therefore taken from the red band (665 nm) at low to moderate concentrations and from the near-infrared band (865 nm) at high concentrations, with a smooth weighted transition between the two. The same approach is used for the Aquascope turbidity (TUR) product, with the turbidity calibration of Nechad et al. (2009).

Nechad, B., Ruddick, K. G., & Neukermans, G. (2009). Calibration and validation of a generic multisensor algorithm for mapping of turbidity in coastal waters. Proc. SPIE 7473, Remote Sensing of the Ocean, Sea Ice, and Large Water Regions 2009, 74730H.

Nechad, B., Ruddick, K. G., & Park, Y. (2010). Calibration and validation of a generic multisensor algorithm for mapping of total suspended matter in turbid waters. Remote Sensing of Environment, 114(4), 854-866.

Novoa, S., Doxaran, D., Ody, A., Vanhellemont, Q., Lafon, V., Lubac, B., & Gernez, P. (2017). Atmospheric corrections and multi-conditional algorithm for multi-sensor remote sensing of suspended particulate matter in low-to-high turbidity levels coastal waters. Remote Sensing, 9(1), 61.

title: CLIMTAG Precipitation Annual Indicator
description:
The *CLIMTAG Precipitation* indicator represents the precipitation derived from ERA5 reanalysis (past) and CMIP6 climate projections (future) under SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, and SSP5-8.5 scenarios.
Annual map (ANNUAL_MAP): annual precipitation sum (mm/year) as spatial GeoTIFFs at reference years 1996â2086 (every 10 years), with ensemble percentiles P10/P25/median/P75/P90.
 
## Past (ERA5 reference)
Daily precipitation totals are fetched from the ERA5 reanalysis (CDS) for the reference temporal extent (1981â2010) window covers the historical anchor). The daily timeseries is temporally aggregated to annual or dekadal sums. A climatology is then computed using a sliding window centred on each reference year. The ERA5 historical reference climatology is downscaled to ~30 arc-second resolution using the GMTED2010 orography dataset. Spatially varying sensitivity parameters for orography (Î²_oro) and distance from the coastline (Î²_coast) are estimated from a ~180 km rolling-window ordinary least-squares regression applied to the coarse ERA5 field, and are used to correct for sub-grid elevation and coastal gradients not resolved at the coarse scale.
 
## Future (CMIP6 projections)
For each CMIP6 model/member, the full projection timeseries is fetched and bias-corrected against ERA5 using empirical quantile delta mapping: this is done for each future timestep according its percentile within a sliding-window cumulative distribution function of the future biased timeseries (30-year window, 5-year step), and the correction is applied according to this percentile rank. Therefore, the bias for each percentile rank is calculated from difference between model historical quantiles and the ERA5 quantiles (after upscaling to the model grid) over the same reference period (1981â2010). The bias correction procedure is done separately for each month of the year using 3-month pooling windows to stabilise tail estimation. The corrected timeseries are then temporally aggregated and a climatology is computed over the same 30-year sliding window. Results are warped to a common 1Â° grid before ensemble statistics (P10, P25, median, P75, P90) are computed across all model members. The final projected climatologies are produced by a delta-mapping approach that combines the coarse-scale ensemble signal with the downscaled ERA5 field.

title: Aquascope sea surface temperature (SST), level-3, 30 m, daily
description:
Sea surface temperature (SST) is the temperature of the ocean's surface layer. Thermal infrared sensors measure the temperature of the skin of the sea surface. With their high spatial resolution, Landsat SST products show coastal and estuarine detail that coarser sensors miss, such as river plumes, fronts, and the warm-water discharges of power plants. The products in this collection are derived from Landsat 8 and Landsat 9 TIRS images at 30 m (100 m native thermal resolution); each input image results in one output product.

The products are based on the standard level-2 surface temperature product of the U.S. Geological Survey (Landsat Collection 2 Level-2), retrieved from the TIRS thermal infrared band 10 with a single-channel algorithm that corrects for the atmosphere using reanalysis profiles. Aquascope applies the USGS quality information to keep only reliable water pixels and maps the result onto a regular grid (level 3). SST is given in kelvin (K).

title: EOCIS Arctic Monthly Gridded Sea Ice Thickness Product from CryoSat-2
description: The sea ice products provide a 5x5 km grid of Arctic sea ice thickness (for the whole Arctic region and of 17 sub-regions), delivered as NetCDF files.  EOCIS sea ice thickness NetCDF products are generated monthly by the Centre for Polar Observation and Modelling (CPOM) from radar altimetry measurements taken from the ESA CryoSAT-2 satellite during the winter months (Oct-Apr). Sea ice thickness is only reliably measured from satellite radar altimetry during the winter months. During summer, melt ponds can form on the sea ice floes making it difficult for the satellite to differentiate between floes and leads, and hence calculate sea ice freeboard (and subsequently thickness). Measurement during summer months using radar altimetry is an area of active research (Landy et al, 2022) but is not yet operationally processed.

title: EOCIS Soil Moisture Africa v2.3.1
description:
This dataset contains Africa-wide soil moisture and related water balance variables produced within the Earth Observation Climate Information Service (EOCIS) project.

The product is derived using the JULES land surface model, forced with TAMSAT satellite rainfall estimates and other meteorological variables from the NCEP reanalysis, and tuned to NASA SMAP satellite soil moisture observations. Data are provided at the daily scale, from 1983-01-01 to present (latency around 7 days) at 0.25 degrees by 0.25 degrees spatial resolution.
producing_org_raw: University of Reading / TAMSAT; Earth Observation Climate Information Service (EOCIS)
keywords_raw: Soil Moisture; Africa

title: EOCIS Sea-Surface Temperatures V3
description: This dataset provides daily-mean sea surface temperatures (SST), presented on global 0.05° latitude-longitude grid, spanning 1980 to present. This is a Level 4 product, with gaps between available daily observations filled by statistical means.  The SST CCI Analysis product contains estimates of daily mean SST and sea ice concentration. Each SST value has an associated uncertainty estimate. The dataset has been produced as part of the version 3 Climate Data Record (CDR) produced by the European Space Agency (ESA) Climate Change Initiative Sea Surface Temperature project (ESA SST_cci). The CDR accurately maps the surface temperature of the global oceans over the period 1980 to 2021 using observations from many satellites, with a high degree of independence from in situ measurements. The data provide independently quantified SSTs to a quality suitable for climate research.  Data from 2022 onwards are provided as an Interim Climate Data Record (ICDR) and will be updated daily at one month behind present. The Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S) funded the development of the ICDR extension and production of the ICDR during 2022. From 2023 onwards the production of the ICDR is funded by the UK Earth Observation Climate Information Service (EOCIS) and Marine and Climate Advisory Service (MCAS).
producing_org_raw: Met Office; Earth Observation Climate Information Service (EOCIS)
keywords_raw: Oceans; Ocean Temperature; Sea Surface Temperature

title: ERA5 Re-analysis (Repacked)
description:
The objectives of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts ERA5 project are to produce and promote use of a comprehensive set of global analyses describing the state of the atmosphere, land and ocean-wave conditions from 1979 to present. The ERA5 project builds on the previous work undertaken by the ERA-15, ERA-40 and ERA-Interim projects. ERA5 is continuously updated at ECMWF, with initial products upto 5 days behind the present day issued as ERA5t ahead of review and final release as the ERA5 data, typically 2 months behind the present month.

This collection of ERA5 data has been repacked without quantised compression for use with the EDS AI projects High5 and FRAME-FM (14th January 2026). This is not a complete record of ERA5 data at CEDA. Further details of the nature of subsetting to follow.

CEDA Catalogue Record: https://catalogue.ceda.ac.uk/uuid/7b64cf24f47f4b1aa499339c5a576be1/

title: ESA Land Cover Climate Change Initiative (CCI): Global Land Cover Maps
description: As part of the ESA Land Cover Climate Change Initiative (CCI) project a new set of Global Land Cover Maps have been produced. These maps are available at 300m spatial resolution for each year between 1992 and 2015. Each pixel value corresponds to the classification of a land cover class defined based on the UN Land Cover Classification System (LCCS). The reliability of the classifications made are documented by the four quality flags (decribed further in the Product User Guide) that accompany these maps. Data are provided in both NetCDF and GeoTiff format.

title: UK Climate Projections (UKCP18)
description: Regional climate model projections produced as part of the UK Climate Projection 2018 (UKCP18) project. The data produced by the Met Office Hadley Centre provides information on changes in climate for the UK until 2080, downscaled to a high resolution (12km), helping to inform adaptation to a changing climate. The projections cover Europe and a 100 year period, 1981-2080, for a high emissions scenario, RCP8.5. Each projection provides an example of climate variability in a changing climate, which is consistent across climate variables at different times and spatial locations. This dataset contains 12km data for the United Kingdom, the Isle of Man and the Channel Islands provided on the Ordnance Survey's British National Grid.
